entry.title: 6th X-Phi Conference in Cagliari
entry.content:
Attending and presenting Poster at the 6th European Experimental Philosophy Conference

The 6th edition of the X-Phi Conference took place in Cagliari last week. It was hosted by the University of Cagliari from the 8th to the 11th September.

I had the opportunity to present my research on the interspecies relationship between humans and animals in poster format. You can take a closer look at the poster on the right.

This research forms part of a larger project called The Animal Dilemmas Project, in which we investigate how people perceive non-human moral entities in the context of dilemma-based decision-making.

For this poster presentation, I developed a mobile-friendly model of the dilemma-based trials that participants undertook. You can find it here.

The organisation of the conference was very good. The organising committee was very attentive to the demands of the speakers and adjusted some time slots accordingly. Moreover, on our last day, we were able to enjoy a tour of the city.

Speaking of the city, I was not expecting it to be so mountainous. However, it certainly left its mark, as you can see in the picture. We also enjoyed some beautiful sunsets and good food.

Overall, it was great to share the progress of my projects with such a well-known circle of people who share my research interests. I’m looking forward to the 7th X-phi next year!
entry.summary: The 6th edition of the European Experimental Philosophy Conference

entry.title: Orientation Days Fulbright 2026-2027 cohort
entry.content:
Three days orientation sessions for the next year Fulbright grantees

Last week, I had the pleasure of attending the Fulbright Association Orientation Days in Madrid.

I’m one of the selected grantees for the 2026-2027 cohort, and I’ll be continuing my PhD research in the US next year. My work on Reasonableness will continue at Georgetown Law, under the supervision of Professor Kevin Tobia.

A huge thank you to the Fulbright Spain for organizing such structured, fun, and collaborative sessions. With around 80 new Fulbrighters in this cohort, from predoctoral researchers to teaching assistants, graduates, and artists, it would have been easy to feel lost in the crowd. But the team made a genuine effort to foster real connections, not just based on where we’re headed, but also on our academic backgrounds and the type of grant we each have. That personal touch made a big difference, and I think it’ll help a lot once we’re all spread across the U.S.

It’s a real pleasure to become part of this community. Looking forward to meeting everyone again on the other side of the Atlantic! 🦅🦅
entry.summary: Three days orientation sessions for the next year Fulbright grantees

entry.title: My three-month research visit at the University of Oxford

link.title: My three-month research visit at the University of Oxford

entry.content:
Visiting the NEUROSEC team at the University of Oxford

Between April and June of this year, I undertook a short research visit to the Design Bioethics Lab (DBL) in the Neuroscience, Ethics and Society (NEUROSEC) group, working under the supervision of Dr Kathryn Francis. This lab is located in what they call “uphill,” in the Department of Psychiatry, at the Warneford Hospital. I have very fond memories of this experience from start to finish. From day one, the DBL team made me feel right at home; they welcomed me, showed me the facilities, and we got to work. Afterwards, we went for drinks and got to know each other better. I was a little nervous at the start of my visit, as I think living abroad can be scary; however, once I had met the team and seen how they worked, all my fears disappeared.

The DBL team meets weekly to discuss the progress and any obstacles in their projects. During my stay, this was especially helpful because it let us work together to find solutions—or at least better understand the issues we faced. I also appreciated getting insights into how the lab works. The day-to-day nature of teamwork, the variety of tasks, and the sense of unity I experienced within the DBL team are things that I have valued and tried to bring back to Spain with me.

I am currently in my third year of a PhD at the University of Granada, Spain, under the supervision of Dr Ivar Rodríguez Hannikainen (Moral Science Lab). My research focuses on investigating how we make moral judgements towards non-human animals and the environment. During my time at Oxford, I focused on developing and refining an experimental design to understand the moral mechanisms people use when deciding which animals and plants to prioritise. I also worked on the theoretical and methodological framework for a manuscript that Dr Francis and I are writing together.

My research lies at the intersection of experimental philosophy and moral psychology. I study what we mean by ‘morally valuable’ and analyse the psychological mechanisms associated with this moral judgement. The DBL team works precisely on this. We shared questions and methods—collaborating with them was the perfect fit.

During my stay, I also had two opportunities to present my work. The first, at the start of my visit to the NEUROSEC team, enabled me to consolidate and reconsider certain aspects of my theoretical background. This allowed me to develop a much more realistic, well-considered prototype for an experiment measuring the effect of choice history on our moral preferences. The second presentation, at a Philosophical Moral Psychology Lab meeting towards the end of my stay, helped me to identify which analyses were clear and which required further elaboration. I would like to thank the Moral Philosophy Lab for allowing me to present my work and for including me in their general lab meetings.

While these academic experiences were enriching, I believe that the visit’s value went beyond these research milestones. Oxford itself provides the ideal space for working from different places, especially when one is stuck with a question or obstacle. Some days, I would work in old city-centre libraries such as the Radcliffe Camera and the Bodleian Library; other days, I would simply move on to newer ones like the Humanities Library. I also loved walking through the city’s parks and Botanic Garden, or exploring the city’s museums and colleges.

Our collaboration did not end the day I finished my stay. Dr Francis and I have kept in touch and we regularly meet up to work on this project and discuss future ones. For anyone considering applying for a research visit with the DBL group, my only advice is… learn the bus times to get to the Warneford Hospital because sometimes they would just magically disappear. Joking aside, be proactive in offering your help with tasks—and do not skip the after-work drinks!

Overall, I am very grateful to Dr Francis for her thoughtful care and guidance, as well as to all the members of the DBL and the entire NEUROSEC group. I am also thankful to my supervisor, Dr Hannikainen, for his support and for funding my stay through his project, and to the University of Granada for helping to cover some of the expenses of this visit.

I feel that I have grown in self-confidence. This experience challenged me to step out of my comfort zone and explore a new country, university, and way of working. Unexpectedly (or perhaps not), this led me to develop a sense of belonging and form professional and personal connections that continue to this day.

I still have vivid memories of the sunsets, the river, and the student atmosphere in the city. It feels as though I was there only last week.
entry.summary: Three-month research visit at the University of Oxford and some thoughts about it

entry.title: I’ve Been Awarded a Fulbright Scholarship!

link.title: I’ve Been Awarded a Fulbright Scholarship!

entry.content:
I got the Fulbright Scholarship for next the year!

This year I decided to apply for the “Fulbright Foundation grant” to conduct a research stay in the United States during the next academic year. And I got into the local news!

My project focuses on analyzing the concept of reasonableness as a social heuristic. But what do we really mean by being reasonable? Many of our everyday and collective moral decisions—such as meat consumption, how we treat certain social groups, or our attention to the environment—revolve around this normative threshold: the reasonable. Yet, despite being such a pervasive standard in our daily lives, we know surprisingly little about how it takes shape in our minds and, more importantly, how it guides our moral behavior.

My Fulbright project addresses precisely this gap. I am investigating whether reasonableness functions as a social heuristic—that is, as a shared mental shortcut we use to make moral decisions quickly and efficiently. In this sense, reasonableness would point neither to perfect or ideal behavior, nor merely to what is common or average, but rather to something “good enough”: demanding enough to avoid moral condemnation, yet flexible enough to be achievable without incurring significant personal, effort-related, or time-related costs.

Recently, we have been exploring the concept of reasonableness through experimental jurisprudence, and we have observed that reasonableness is perceived as more morally permissible and more intuitive (more cognitively accessible) than other normative criteria, which could suggest the presence of such a heuristic. These findings are detailed in this project and were also presented last July in Norwich.

In the United States, specifically at Georgetown Law, I will experimentally test whether people’s actions follow a pattern of reasonableness and whether the most efficient solutions in various behavioral games—both at the group and individual levels—tend to be organize precisely around this standard. I will conduct this research under the guidance of Professor K. Tobia. Professor Tobia is a leading international figure in the field of experimental jurisprudence, a discipline that has integrated empirical methods to study concepts with long-standing philosophical and legal traditions –such as reasonableness.

I must admit I am especially excited to carry out this research with such leading and influential figures in the field. In addition, I am honored by the prospect of joining the vibrant community of the Fulbright Foundation.
entry.summary: Awarded a Fulbright Scholarship for the upcoming academic year and was mentioned in the 'Granada Hoy' newspapers!

entry.title: Legal Interpretation and Moral Reasoning Workshop

link.title: Legal Interpretation and Moral Reasoning Workshop

entry.content:
Reflecting on the 2025 Legal Interpretation and Moral Reasoning Workshop

From Wednesday, 5th to Friday, 7th of November 2025, we gathered at the University of Granada for the Workshop of Legal Interpretation and Moral Reasoning.

As one of the organisers, I couldn’t have been more pleased with how it turned out. Over these three days, the discussions were rich, the questions sharp, and the atmosphere genuinely collaborative. The workshop brought together 13 speakers from philosophy, law, and psychology who shared fascinating perspectives on the connections between legal interpretation, cognitive science, and moral reasoning. It was inspiring to see how each contribution opened new ways of thinking about how people make sense of rules, norms, and moral principles across different contexts.

Beyond the sessions themselves, we also enjoyed some wonderful moments together outside the workshop, sharing dinners, exploring Granada’s atmosphere, and even watching some fire performances. These moments made the event not only intellectually stimulating but also deeply human and memorable.

A huge thank you to all our speakers and to my fantastic co-organizers, Rosa López and Ivar Rodríguez Hannikainen, for making this such an nice experience!
entry.summary: 2025 Legal Interpretation and Moral Reasoning Workshop, organized at the University of Granada

entry.title: EASP Summer School 2025
entry.content:
Reflecting on the EASP Summer School 2025 in Canterbury

This summer I had the chance to take part in the EASP Summer School in Canterbury. It was two weeks full of learning, discussions, and getting to know people from many different places and backgrounds.

I joined the Moral Psychology and Artificial Intelligence workstream with Jim Everett and Madeline (“Gracie”) Reinecke. We looked at AI not just as a technology, but as something that raises deep questions about our values, our decisions, and the way we relate to each other in a world where machines are increasingly present. I found it both challenging and refreshing to think about how psychology, philosophy and AI come together, and how research can engage with these questions in practice.

Outside the classroom, there were plenty of activities that made the experience even richer: from exploring Canterbury to just spending time with others over a meal or during the organized events. Those moments mattered as much as the academic side, because they made it easy to connect, exchange ideas, and feel part of a wider community.

Looking back, I’m grateful for the balance of learning, collaboration, and simply sharing experiences. The summer school wasn’t just about the science, but also about the people, the conversations, and the projects that will keep going long after. Thanks to everyone who made this possible.
entry.summary: 2025 Summer School of the European Association of Social Psychology, hosted at the University of Kent

entry.title: PHAIR 2025 in Edinburgh
entry.content:
The PHAIR 2025 Animal Advocacy Conference in Edinburgh

This July I had the chance to attend PHAIR 2025 in Edinburgh, my very first time at this conference, organized by the PHAIR Society. The Society for the Psychology of Human-Animal Intergroup Relations (PHAIR) is an association dedicated to building bridges between psychology and animal advocacy, bringing together researchers, advocates, and practitioners who care about the moral standing of animals and how we should act on it. The conference reflected this mission beautifully: it wasn’t only academics presenting their work, but also activists sharing practical perspectives. That combination made for a unique experience.

The setting in Edinburgh couldn’t have been better. The city itself was beautiful, and the atmosphere of the conference was warm, energizing, and incredibly well-organized. I met so many fantastic people. One of the highlights was meeting Peter Singer, a philosopher whose work has shaped the field for decades. I also had the chance to connect with others whose research has been central to my own, like Josh Rottman, Matti Wilks, and Charlie Crimston.

Overall, PHAIR 2025 was an amazing mix of rigorous discussion and real-world engagement. It was a privilege to be part of a community where psychology and advocacy come together. Can’t wait for the 2027 one!
entry.summary: The PHAIR 2025 Animal Advocacy Conference in Edinburgh

entry.title: 5th Euro Xphi Conference in Norwich
entry.content:
Attending and presenting at the 5th European Experimental Philosophy Conference

Last week I had the chance to attend the EuroX-Phi 2025 conference at the University of East Anglia in Norwich. The city itself was a lovely surprise, quiet, beautiful, and full of character, and the atmosphere of the event was just as welcoming. I got to meet some really nice people, exchange ideas informally, and enjoy the feeling of being part of this lifely community working on similar projects.

The conference also featured some fantastic keynotes, including a talk by Josh Knobe that sparked a lot of discussion. I presented my own project, Practical Reason: Frequency and Evaluation Effects on Judgments of Normality and Reasonableness, which is part of my broader project on how people think about normality and practical reasoning.

It was great to share my work in this setting, get feedback, and see how it connects with other ongoing debates. Overall, it was an inspiring few days, both intellectually and personally.
entry.summary: The 5th edition of the European Experimental Philosophy Conference

entry.title: 2025 BioXPhi Summit in Basel
entry.content:
Attending and presenting at the 2025 BioXPhi Summit in Basel

I recently attended the 2025 Basel-Oxford-NUS BioXPhi Summit, and it was an incredible experience. Held from June 26–27 at the University of Basel, the summit brought together researchers from around the world to explore the emerging field of Bioxphi, where philosophy, moral psychology, and bioethics intersect.

The sessions were fascinating, and I particularly enjoyed meeting Matti Wilks, whose work on the moral circle and animal ethics has greatly influenced my PhD project.

Basel itself was stunning. The city, the river, and its historic streets made for a beautiful backdrop to the summit.

Overall, the summit was a perfect combination of learning, discussion, and informal networking. I’m very grateful to the organizers, speacilly Christian Rodriguez Perez for creating such a thoughtful and well-run event, and to everyone I met for sharing their ideas. It was a great reminder of how exciting this new area of research is and how much there is to learn.
entry.summary: The 2025 edition of the Experimental philosophical bioethics ("BioXPhi") Summit

entry.title: Vienna Summer School 2024
entry.content:
Stratégies numériques pour la formation doctorale en sciences humaines et sociales

Organised by UNIMED and the University of Vienna, this second summer school took place within the Erasmus+ project RAQMYAT (“Digital Strategies for Doctoral Training in the Humanities and Social Sciences”). It ran online from 17 to 20 September 2024 and continued in person in Vienna from 23 to 27 September 2024.

Throughout the week, we explored how digital tools and experimental methods can enrich research in the humanities. Workshops on data management, online collaboration, and digital analysis opened new ways of thinking about my own work. I realised how much philosophical research can benefit from engaging with digital humanities and psychology, especially when studying moral reasoning and human moral behaviour.

The group brought together researchers from across the Mediterranean and beyond, creating a lovely space for exchange and collaboration. Vienna, perhaps the most beautiful city I’ve been to, provided the perfect backdrop for such an inspiring week. Outside the sessions, sharing meals and discovering Vienna together made the experience even more rewarding. Those informal moments turned discussions into friendships and ideas into possible projects.

At the end of the week, I was honoured with the Best Research Poster Award, a recognition that reflected both the effort put into my project and the collaborative spirit that defined the entire week.
entry.summary: 2024 Summer School of RAQMYAT Project in Vienna, Austria, organized by the UNIMED and the University of Vienna.
